description: Metal categorisation, working properties, named alloys, stock forms and protective finishes.
content_html:
Ferrous vs Non-Ferrous

Metals are divided into two fundamental categories. Ferrous metals contain iron. They are generally strong and magnetic, but rust when exposed to moisture and oxygen unless protected. Non-ferrous metals contain no iron. They resist corrosion naturally and are non-magnetic—making them valuable in electrical applications (where magnetic interference must be avoided) and in marine environments. The third category, alloys, are mixtures of two or more metals (or a metal and another element) engineered to achieve properties neither constituent has alone.

Key Fact

Ferrous metals contain iron and tend to rust; non-ferrous metals do not contain iron and resist corrosion naturally. Mild steel (ferrous) and aluminium (non-ferrous) are the most commonly used metals in manufacturing industry.

Ferrous Metals — Named Examples

Cast iron contains 2–4% carbon, making it very hard and brittle. It cannot be bent or forged—it fractures rather than deforming. Used for machine tool beds, drain covers and engine blocks, where rigidity under compression is needed and brittleness is acceptable. It has excellent compressive strength but low tensile strength.

Mild steel (also called low-carbon steel) contains 0.1–0.3% carbon. It is the most widely used engineering material in the world. Tensile strength is approximately 400–500 MPa. It is ductile, malleable and weldable—but rusts readily and must be painted, galvanised or powder-coated for outdoor use. Used in structural beams, car bodies, pipework and general fabrication.

Medium and high carbon steels have progressively more carbon (0.3–1.4%), giving greater hardness and wear resistance but reduced ductility and weldability. High carbon steel is used for cutting tools, springs and high-stress components. It can be heat-treated (hardened and tempered) to control the balance of hardness and toughness.

Non-Ferrous Metals — Named Examples

Aluminium has a density of approximately 2.7 g/cm³—about one third the density of steel. It naturally forms an oxide layer that prevents further corrosion. Good conductor of heat and electricity. Used in aircraft frames, food cans, window frames and heat exchangers. Can be anodised to enhance its oxide layer and add colour. Recycling aluminium uses only around 5% of the energy needed to smelt virgin aluminium from bauxite.

Copper is an excellent electrical conductor (second only to silver) and has high thermal conductivity. It is ductile enough to be drawn into fine wire and malleable enough to be beaten into shape. Used in electrical wiring, plumbing pipes and heat exchangers. Copper weathers to a green patina (copper carbonate) that actually protects the underlying metal.

Common Alloys

Alloys are engineered mixtures. The specification names brass and bronze specifically:

  • Brass—copper (roughly 65%) and zinc (roughly 35%). Harder than copper alone, non-sparking, and corrosion-resistant. Used in musical instruments, plumbing fittings, electrical connectors and decorative hardware. Machines cleanly with a good surface finish.
  • Bronze—copper and tin (historically around 88% copper, 12% tin). Harder and more corrosion-resistant than copper alone. Used in bearings, marine propellers, bells and sculpture. The tin content makes it harder to machine than brass but gives superior strength for load-bearing applications.
Key Fact

Brass = copper + zinc. Bronze = copper + tin. Both are corrosion-resistant alloys derived from copper. Brass is commonly used for plumbing fittings and musical instruments; bronze for marine propellers and bearings.

Working Properties

Designers and engineers select metals based on specific working properties. These are the key terms the exam tests:

PropertyDefinitionHigh-value example
Tensile strengthResist pulling forcesMild steel (~400–500 MPa)
HardnessResist surface indentation or scratchingHigh carbon steel
DuctilityDrawn into wireCopper, aluminium
MalleabilityBeaten or pressed into shape without crackingAluminium, copper
ToughnessAbsorb impact energy without fracturingMild steel
ElasticityReturn to original shape after load removedSpring steel

Metals are supplied in standard stock forms to minimise waste when cutting components to size. Common forms include:

  • Sheet—flat rolled metal, typically 0.5–3 mm thick for mild steel and aluminium. Used for pressed body panels, enclosures and cans.
  • Bar (flat/square)—solid rectangular or square cross-section. Used for structural brackets, levers and frames.
  • Rod (round bar)—solid circular cross-section, turned in a lathe to produce shafts and pins.
  • Tube—hollow circular section. High strength-to-weight ratio because material is placed at maximum distance from the neutral axis. Used for cycle frames, scaffold poles and handrails.
  • Angle—L-shaped cross-section. Provides stiffness to a structure when welded or bolted at corners. Used in frames, brackets and shelving.

Ferrous metals must be protected from moisture and oxygen to prevent rust. Common methods include:

  • Galvanising—dipping steel in molten zinc. The zinc acts as a sacrificial coating: it corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel beneath. Used for outdoor structures, car body panels undercoating and corrugated roofing.
  • Powder coating—electrostatically applying a dry polymer powder to a metal surface, then curing it in an oven. Produces a hard, even coating in a wide range of colours. More durable than conventional liquid paint and produces less VOC waste.
  • Painting—the simplest surface treatment. Requires proper surface preparation (degreasing, priming) to adhere well. Relatively low cost but needs re-application as the paint chips or weathers.
  • Anodising (aluminium)—an electrochemical process that thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminium. The thickened layer is then dyed. Produces a decorative and very wear-resistant surface. Used on window frames, bicycle components and consumer electronics.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions on metals, always use the precise property name (tensile strength, ductility, malleability) rather than vague terms like “strong” or “flexible.” For 6-mark and 12-mark questions, link each property to a specific product application—for example: “aluminium’s low density of 2.7 g/cm³ makes it suitable for aircraft fuselages where minimising mass is critical to fuel efficiency.” For corrosion protection questions, name the specific process (galvanising, powder coating, anodising) rather than just writing “paint it”—and explain the mechanism. For Q6 on metals, a strong response discusses at least two named metals, their working properties, stock forms, and one finish or processing method with a real product context.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ferrous metals contain iron (e.g. mild steel, cast iron) and rust unless protected. Non-ferrous metals (e.g. aluminium, copper) do not contain iron and resist corrosion naturally. Alloys (brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin) are engineered mixtures for superior properties.
  • Key working properties to know: tensile strength (mild steel ~400–500 MPa), ductility, malleability, toughness, hardness and elasticity. Each maps to specific applications.
  • Stock forms (sheet, bar, rod, tube, angle) allow designers to select the most efficient cross-section. Ferrous metals are protected by galvanising, powder coating, painting or plating; aluminium is anodised.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following metals is non-ferrous?
A) Cast iron
B) Mild steel
C) High carbon steel
D) Copper
State what is meant by the term ductility in relation to metals.
practice_questions.marks: The ability of a material to be drawn into wire or thin sections without breaking [2 marks]. (1 mark for partial answer: ‘can be stretched’ without further qualification.)

practice_questions.text: Identify the two metals that are combined to produce brass, and describe one property that makes brass suitable for plumbing fittings.
practice_questions.marks: Copper [1] and zinc [1]. One mark for a relevant property with brief reason, e.g. brass is corrosion-resistant so it does not degrade in contact with water [1], or brass is non-sparking so it is safe around gases [1], or brass machines cleanly for precision threaded fittings [1]. (3 marks total.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why tube is often preferred over solid round bar for cycle frame construction, even though both are the same material.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Tube provides a high strength-to-weight ratio [1] because material is placed at maximum distance from the neutral axis, making bending resistance high relative to mass [1]
• Solid bar of the same diameter would be much heavier [1] which would reduce performance and increase energy required to accelerate the bike [1]
• Tube can be butted (thicker at stress points, thinner in the middle) to further optimise material use [1]
(2 marks per developed point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is producing mild steel garden furniture for sale without any surface finish. Explain, with reference to the product’s function and environment, why this is problematic and recommend a suitable finishing process, justifying your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that mild steel contains iron and will rust in outdoor conditions where moisture and oxygen are present, degrading the structure and appearance over time. Recommends a specific finish (e.g. powder coating) with justified reasoning linking the finish mechanism to the product context (electrostatically applied polymer cures to a durable, weather-resistant surface available in a wide colour range; more durable than liquid paint and produces less VOC). Mentions that galvanising is an alternative for structural outdoor steel.
Secure: Identifies the rust problem and recommends a named finish with some explanation of the mechanism.
Developing: States mild steel rusts and recommends ‘painting’ without explaining surface preparation or process.
Emerging: Identifies that the metal will corrode but cannot name or explain a finishing method.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using aluminium rather than mild steel for a bicycle frame. Consider material properties, processing and environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides. Aluminium advantages: density ~2.7 g/cm³ vs steel ~7.8 g/cm³ gives significantly lower mass; naturally corrosion-resistant so no protective finish needed (cost and environmental saving); can be anodised for decorative effect; high recycled content possible. Aluminium disadvantages: lower tensile strength per unit volume than steel (aluminium ~100–300 MPa vs mild steel ~400–500 MPa) so larger cross-sections or alloy grades needed; aluminium work-hardens and can crack under repeated fatigue loading; welding aluminium requires specialist TIG process and inert shielding gas. Reaches a reasoned judgement.
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side with property-specific detail; judgement present.
Developing: Points on both sides but limited development.
Emerging: Mainly one side or superficial.

knowledge_checks.q: Why does cast iron fracture rather than bend when a large force is applied?
options: Its high carbon content makes it hard but brittle
It has a very low tensile strength only above 200°C
Applying a polymer powder coating and curing it in an oven
Dipping steel in molten zinc to create a sacrificial protective coating
Electrochemically thickening the oxide layer on aluminium
Painting steel with a rust-resistant primer

knowledge_checks.q: Aluminium has a density of approximately _____ g/cm³.
The ability of a material to return to its original shape after a load is removed is called _____.
Match each metal or alloy to its composition or key property:
right: Ferrous metal with ~0.1–0.3% carbon; ductile and weldable

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between ferrous and non-ferrous metals?
flashcard_questions.a: Ferrous metals contain iron; non-ferrous metals do not.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate tensile strength of mild steel?
What is the approximate density of aluminium?
Which two metals are combined to make brass?
Which two metals are combined to make bronze?
What property describes a metal's ability to be drawn into wire without breaking?
Why is cast iron unsuitable for components that must bend under load?
flashcard_questions.a: Its high carbon content makes it brittle — it fractures rather than deforms.

flashcard_questions.q: What process coats steel in molten zinc to provide sacrificial corrosion protection?
What electrochemical process thickens the oxide layer on aluminium and allows it to be dyed?
Why does a hollow tube cross-section give a higher strength-to-weight ratio than a solid bar of the same material?
flashcard_questions.a: Material is placed at maximum distance from the neutral axis, maximising bending resistance per unit of mass.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does aluminium resist corrosion without a painted or galvanised finish?
flashcard_questions.a: It naturally forms a thin, protective oxide layer on its surface.

flashcard_questions.q: What carbon content range defines mild steel?

glossary_terms.definition: Metals that contain iron as their main component and are typically magnetic; they are prone to rusting unless protected.
Metals that do not contain iron as their main component; they are generally corrosion-resistant and non-magnetic.
A material made by combining two or more metals (or a metal and another element) to achieve properties superior to either constituent alone.
The ability of a material to withstand a stretching (tensile) force without breaking.
The ability of a material to be drawn into wire or thin sections without breaking.
